rationale: A wins because it keeps four clean, pitchable lanes without smuggling in outside context. Its best line, "Calm has 4 million paying subscribers. Its insurer deal hands the app free to 25 million," turns the announcement into a real business-model question. B has sharper teeth in "The company that sells the app paid for the study that says the app works," but then dirties the file with unsupported claims like "demand for care exceeds clinician supply" and "on the plan's dime." That is how good instincts become reporter bait in the wrong direction.
gaps_in_A: "pointing to a randomized trial as the reason" overstates payer rationale; the update says the study exists, not that insurers used it as the reason for coverage.

The service angle, "Your health plan may now include Calm Premium at no cost," only works if the three insurers and activation path can be named. A flags that, but it is still the flimsiest kept angle.
"Calm's trial shows an 18% anxiety-score drop" is careful, but it could have separated the funding-bias/investigative version more explicitly instead of folding it into methodology.
The refused regulatory angle says it belongs in uncomfortable questions, but the questions never actually ask what coverage status does or does not imply regulatorily.
gaps_in_B: "demand for care exceeds clinician supply" is invented. B even refuses a similar crisis/clinician-supply peg later, which makes the miss harder to forgive.
"agree to reimburse" and "on the plan's dime" imply payment mechanics the update explicitly withholds. Covered benefit is not the same as known reimbursement.

The category angle and insurer angle are too close: "consumer wellness subscription crossing into covered-benefit status" and "three national carriers made a purchasing decision" are cousins wearing different jackets.
"employer and payer channels" drags employers into the business-model angle without supplied facts. The update says insurers, not employers.
